pages.text: Long ago, all the stories in the world belonged to Nyame, the Creator. Ananse the spider spun a silver web and climbed up to the heavens to ask Nyame for them. “What price will you pay for my stories?” Nyame asked.
sentences: Long ago, all the stories in the world belonged to Nyame, the Creator.
Ananse the spider spun a silver web and climbed up to the heavens to ask Nyame for them.
“What price will you pay for my stories?” Nyame asked.
pages.alt: Small clever Ananse having climbed his shimmering silver spider-web up to the heavens, looking up respectfully at Nyame, the Creator, in golden kente robes.

pages.text: Nyame set four hard tasks. “Bring me Ɔnini the python, Mmɔborɔ, the stinging hornets, Osebo the leopard, and Mmoatia the forest dwarf,” he said. Some storytellers change this list a little.
sentences: “Bring me Ɔnini the python, Mmɔborɔ, the stinging hornets, Osebo the leopard, and Mmoatia the forest dwarf,” he said.
Some storytellers change this list a little.
pages.alt: Nyame, the Creator, seated in radiant heavenly clouds holding up four fingers clearly while small Ananse listens attentively below.

pages.text: Ananse went home and asked his wife, Aso, for help. Together they prepared an empty calabash gourd, cool water, and strong vine, because two minds are better than one.
sentences: Ananse went home and asked his wife, Aso, for help.
Together they prepared an empty calabash gourd, cool water, and strong vine, because two minds are better than one.
pages.alt: Ananse and his thoughtful wife Aso sitting together at a wooden table inside their cosy home with an empty calabash gourd and coiled vine, smiling as they plan.

pages.text: In the tale, Ananse sprinkled water like rain so Mmɔborɔ, the stinging hornets, flew into his empty gourd for shelter. Then he measured Ɔnini along a palm branch and outwitted Osebo and Mmoatia the forest dwarf. Never touch or trap real wild animals or hornets!
sentences: In the tale, Ananse sprinkled water like rain so Mmɔborɔ, the stinging hornets, flew into his empty gourd for shelter.
Then he measured Ɔnini along a palm branch and outwitted Osebo and Mmoatia the forest dwarf.
Never touch or trap real wild animals or hornets!
pages.alt: Ananse climbing toward the heavens carrying a closed woven basket and calabash gourd, while far below in the green forest the leopard and python rest free and undisturbed.

pages.text: Ananse climbed his web back to the heavens with all four. Nyame, the Creator, was amazed. “You have done everything I asked,” he said. “From today, the stories are yours, and they shall be called Spider Stories.”
sentences: Ananse climbed his web back to the heavens with all four.
“You have done everything I asked,” he said.
“From today, the stories are yours, and they shall be called Spider Stories.”
pages.alt: Nyame, the Creator, smiling warmly in the heavens and handing a glowing golden carved wooden story-box to joyful Ananse.

pages.text: That is why many Akan people call folktales Anansesɛm, or Spider Stories. When elders tell them in the evening, children gather round to listen and learn.
sentences: That is why many Akan people call folktales Anansesɛm, or Spider Stories.
When elders tell them in the evening, children gather round to listen and learn.
pages.alt: A Ghanaian village elder seated by a warm evening courtyard fire telling an animated story while happy children sit on mats listening in wonder under starry skies.

glossary.definition: In Akan tradition, the Supreme God and Creator of heaven and earth.
Standard Twi name in Ananse tales for the great African rock python.
Traditional Akan folktale name for the stinging hornets.
A small West African forest dwarf in Akan folklore.
A hard-shelled hollow fruit, such as a calabash, dried and used as a container.
